title: Online Fraud, Scams and Staying Safe Online
summary: UPI and OTP scams (tricks to steal your money), fake jobs, loan apps, how to stay safe on social media, and how to report online fraud fast.
sectionRefs: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (cheating, stalking, criminal intimidation)

body.text: Online fraud happens very fast. The stolen money often passes through many bank accounts within minutes. So what you do in the first hour is very important.
Common scams (tricks) to watch out for

items: UPI / OTP fraud: someone calls and says they are from your bank. Or they send a 'collect request' (a request to take money from you) and ask you to approve it. Remember: approving a collect request sends money OUT. It does not bring money in.
Fake job offers: a person says they will give you a job, then asks for money for registration, training or security. Real employers never ask you to pay to get a job.
Loan apps: some apps give a loan in minutes, but first they demand to see your contacts and photos. Later they trouble you. Use only lenders that the RBI (the country's central bank) controls.
Prize or lottery scams: a message says you have won a prize. Then it asks for a fee or your bank details.
Fake customer-care numbers: you search online for a company's helpline. Some numbers in the results are not the company's real number.

body.text: How to stay safe on social media

items: Keep your profile private (only friends can see it). Let strangers see as little as possible.
Never share OTPs (the one-time passwords sent to your phone), your live location, or your ID papers in chats.
Be careful with 'friends' who ask for money or private photos soon after meeting you.
Turn on two-factor authentication (a second check, like an OTP, when you log in) for WhatsApp, Instagram and your email.

body.text: Online stalking, threats and private photos

items: Following someone online again and again (stalking), threatening them, pretending to be someone else, and sharing private photos without permission are all crimes. The IT Act and the criminal law punish them.
Do not delete the proof. Take screenshots. Save profile links and the times of the messages.
Report it at cybercrime.gov.in. A woman in trouble can also call 181.

body.text: What to do first after a money fraud

items: Call the national cyber helpline 1930 at once.
Report it on the official website cybercrime.gov.in.
Tell your bank. Ask them to freeze the payment or the account.
Change your passwords. Turn on two-factor authentication.

body.text: Do not call the scammer again. Never pay any 'release fee' or 'processing charge' to get your money back. That is a second scam.
The 'golden hour' is the short time just after a fraud. If you report within it, you have the best chance of freezing the money before it moves.
You can file a complaint online even if you are not sure it is a crime. Reporting helps you and protects others.
Report at once: helpline 1930 and cybercrime.gov.in

items: Report at once. Call the cyber helpline 1930 and use the portal cybercrime.gov.in.
Reporting in the first hour (the 'golden hour') gives the best chance of freezing the money.

Under the Information Technology Act, 2000: section 66C is identity theft, section 66D is cheating by personation (pretending to be someone else), section 66E is a privacy violation, and section 67 covers obscene material.
Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: cheating is section 318, criminal intimidation is section 351, stalking is section 78, and defamation is section 356.

body.text: RBI rule: report within 3 working days

items: Under RBI rules, if you report an unauthorised electronic transaction within 3 working days, your liability is zero.

body.text: Never share your OTP, PIN, CVV or password

items: Never share an OTP, PIN, CVV or password with anyone.
A UPI PIN sends money out. It never receives money.
Use only digital lending apps that the RBI regulates.
Unregulated loan apps can misuse your contacts and photos.
Sharing someone's private images without their consent is an offence.
A woman in distress can call 181.
If your bank complaint is not resolved, escalate it to the RBI Ombudsman (the officer who handles complaints against banks).

practicalSteps: Act within the first hour if you can.
Call 1930 and file a complaint on cybercrime.gov.in.
Give your bank the transaction number in writing. Ask for a written reply that they received it.
Before you delete anything, save screenshots, transaction IDs, phone numbers and links.
If you do not get the money back, complain to the RBI Ombudsman (an officer who handles complaints against banks).
exceptions: If the loss is small and the bank refuses to act, a consumer or civil case may be faster than a criminal case.
Besides the national website, some states have their own cyber police teams.

faqs.q: Can I get my money back?
faqs.a: Sometimes. If you report the fraud quickly, and the money is still sitting in a bank account, the bank can freeze it and give it back. The longer you wait, the harder it gets.

faqs.q: Will my complaint be kept private?
faqs.a: Yes. For some kinds of cases, the official website lets you report without giving your name. Your details are used to look into the case.

sources.label: Ministry of Electronics and IT (IT Act, 2000)

misconceptions.myth: I can just ask the scammer to give my money back.
misconceptions.fact: Scammers almost never give money back. They often ask for even more. Stop talking to them and report to 1930.
